channel.title: RoofPayback blog
channel.description: Daily articles on U.S. electricity prices and rooftop solar payback, built on EIA and PVWatts data.

item.title: Is Solar Worth It in Cloudy States? What the Numbers Show
item.description: Cloudy states can still see solar pay off when electricity prices are high. See output, prices and payback for the lowest-sunshine states.

item.title: Solar Panels for an Electric Car: How Much Bigger?
item.description: Adding an EV means more kWh per year. See how right-sized solar systems and payback change in four example states, with assumptions stated.

item.title: Solar for High-Usage Homes: Does a Bigger Bill Pay Back Faster?
item.description: Does a high electric bill mean faster solar payback? We compare small, average and large homes in TX, CA, FL and AZ with right-sized systems.

item.title: Solar Panel Degradation: 0.5% vs 0.8% Over 25 Years
item.description: How much output do solar panels lose over 25 years? Compare 0.5% and 0.8% yearly degradation and see the effect on payback and savings in five states.

item.title: Solar Payback If Electricity Prices Keep Rising
item.description: See how 0%, 2.5% and 4% yearly electricity price growth change solar payback and 25-year gain for an example home in five states.

item.title: Solar Cost Per Watt: How Your Quote Changes Payback
item.description: See how solar cost per watt changes payback in Texas, California, Florida, Arizona and New York, and when a cheaper quote really matters for your home.

item.title: Daytime Power Use and Solar Payback: 30%, 40%, 60%
item.description: See how using more solar power during the day changes payback under full and reduced export credits, with model results for California, Texas, Florida and Arizona.

item.title: Electricity Prices in August 2026: What Changed, Where
item.description: U.S. residential electricity averaged 18.16¢/kWh in August 2026. See which states rose or fell most, regional gaps, and what it means for your bill and solar.

item.title: Solar Loan vs. Cash: How Financing Changes Payback
item.description: Loan-financed solar had a higher median installed price than cash in Berkeley Lab data. See how interest changes payback and when savings cover payments.

item.title: Solar Panel Cost by State: Installed Price and Payback
item.description: What do solar panels cost? See Berkeley Lab installed prices per watt and how the same cost pays back faster or slower depending on your state.

item.title: How to Lower Your Electric Bill: Steps That Add Up
item.description: Practical ways to lower your electric bill, with what one saved kWh is worth in each state and when rate plans or solar make sense.

item.title: Can a Solar System Be Too Big? Annual True-Up Explained
item.description: An oversized solar system can produce kWh your utility never credits. See where the waste shows up in sizing tables and how to pick a smarter size.

item.title: Time-of-Use Electricity Rates Explained for Homeowners
item.description: How time-of-use electricity rates work, who they help, who they may cost more, and what to check with your utility, including how solar fits in.

item.title: Does Roof Pitch Matter for Solar? 20° vs. 30° Compared
item.description: Roof pitch changes solar output by only a few percent. See how 20° and 30° compare on south, east, and west roofs, and what it means for payback.

item.title: Where Electricity Prices Are Rising Fastest by State
item.description: EIA July 2026 data shows which states had the biggest residential electricity price increases, which saw drops, and what it means for solar payback.

item.title: Solar Payback Period Explained: What Sets the Number
item.description: Solar payback depends on cost, output, price, export credit and self-use. See real examples by state and why a bigger system is not always better.

item.title: Rising electricity prices: where solar pays back fastest
item.description: Compare electricity prices and solar payback by state: see where a rooftop system pays back fastest, where it is slowest, and why credit rules matter.

item.title: Electricity Prices by U.S. Region: July 2026 Compared
item.description: Compare residential, commercial and industrial electricity prices across EIA regions, from New England to the Pacific, with year-over-year changes.

item.title: Cheapest and Most Expensive States for Electricity
item.description: See which states have the cheapest and most expensive residential electricity, with July 2026 EIA prices, example monthly bills and year-over-year changes.

item.title: Average Electric Bill by State: What 900 kWh Costs
item.description: What 900 kWh of electricity costs each month in every U.S. state at July 2026 EIA average residential prices, and why your real bill differs.

item.title: Best States for Solar Payback: Fastest and Slowest
item.description: Where does home solar pay back fastest? We rank states with one example home and explain why electricity prices matter more than sunshine.

item.title: East- or West-Facing Roof: Is Solar Still Worth It?
item.description: East- or west-facing solar panels made about 14.5% to 14.8% less power than south-facing ones across U.S. states. See where the loss is biggest and smallest.

item.title: Home EV Charging Cost by State: What It Costs in 2026
item.description: What it costs to charge an electric car at home in every state, using July 2026 EIA electricity prices and a 3500 kWh per year example.

item.title: Solar Panels in Winter: Output by State vs. Summer
item.description: How much do solar panels make in winter? Winter vs. summer output per kW for U.S. states, why the gap grows up north, and what it means for net metering.

item.title: U.S. Electricity Prices in July 2026: What Changed
item.description: July 2026 EIA data: U.S. residential power averaged 18.31¢/kWh, up 4.9%. See which states rose or fell, and what it means for bills and solar payback.

item.title: What Is a Kilowatt-Hour and How Much Does One Cost?
item.description: A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is how utilities measure the electricity you use. Learn what it means in plain words and what a kWh costs in each U.S. state.

item.title: Why Electricity Prices Differ So Much by State
item.description: Home electricity ran from 12.72¢ to 48¢ per kWh across states in July 2026. Here is what drives the gap, explained with EIA data.

item.title: Why Homes Pay More for Electricity Than Businesses
item.description: Homes paid 18.31¢/kWh in July 2026 vs 9.77¢/kWh for industry, per EIA. See why delivery costs drive the gap and how it varies by state.

item.title: How many solar panels do I need? Sizing from your electric bill
item.description: A step-by-step way to size a home solar system from your annual kWh, daytime use and local sunshine, with real size-vs-payback tables for four states.

item.title: Is solar still worth it without the 30% federal tax credit?
item.description: The 30% federal solar credit is gone for new systems. We ran payback for every state without it, and compared it with what the credit used to do.
